title: Retail Therapy and the “Treat Yourself” Spiral: When Self-Care Spending Becomes a Coping Mechanism
summary: I thought retail therapy was self-care, until I realized it was self-soothing. Here’s how I learned to tell a real treat from emotional spending.
body_markdown:
## Where the “Treat Yourself” Spiral Comes From


We live in a culture that has fully monetized the concept of self-care. Brands are very good at meeting us in our most stressed, depleted moments and whispering that the solution is something we can buy. A new pair of earrings. A fancy drink. A new lipstick.


While none of these things are inherently bad, the “treat yourself” framing benefits consumerism more than it does us. This trend conflates spending money with taking care of yourself – which keeps us reaching for our wallets every time we feel bad, instead of asking why we feel bad.


That’s not to say buying things is never okay, of course. But there’s a meaningful difference between spending that genuinely nourishes you and spending to avoid, cope with, or numb out from something – like[low self-esteem](https://lifestance.com/condition/low-self-esteem/) , stress, sadness, a lack of fulfillment or excitement about your future, or life circumstances that aren’t working for you and need to change.


In my case, I was using shopping to manage[anxiety](https://lifestance.com/services/anxiety-disorder-treatment/) and burnout I wasn’t ready to face. Every purchase was a small hit of relief that made me feel okay enough to get through another day in a job that was slowly draining me. The thing is that the spending was actually keeping me stuck. It was making an unbearable situation just bearable enough that I didn’t have to do anything about it.


After I left the city and built a life with more freedom and fulfillment – traveling, spending time in nature, flexibility, filling my cup – I could look back and clearly see what had been happening. The caffeine fixes and the fast-fashion hauls weren’t rewards. They were coping mechanisms. Little patches over a bigger problem I wasn’t addressing: a job that I wasn’t happy about, the ongoing stress, and the unpleasant feelings that my situation created.
